list.listitem: Sjogren's syndrome is an autoimmune disorder characterized by lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltration and destruction of salivary, lacrimal, and other exocrine glands.
Key symptoms include dry mouth and dry eye. If clinically suspected, order anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies, CBC, RF, and ANA. C
Manage patients in consultation with an ophthalmologist, dentist and/or rheumatologist as needed. C

Therapies include hydroxychloroquine or methotrexate for musculoskeletal symptoms; exercise, dehydroepiandrosterone, and hydroxychloroquine for fatigue; lubricants, cyclosporine, and pulsed steroids for dry eye; and cevimeline, pilocarpine and rituximab for xerostomia.B

background.definition: (SS) is an autoimmune disease characterized by inflammation of exocrine glands, mainly the lacrimal and salivary glands. It can be present alone (primary) or in combination with other autoimmune diseases (secondary) such asrheumatoid arthritis orsystemic lupus erythematosus.

list.listitem: The estimated annual incidence rate in the US is about 0.004%.
The few epidemiological studies of primary SS that exist suggest wide variation in disease prevalence, ranging from 0.02% to 6%.
The cost of the treatment of SS is almost double compared with healthy controls.
Disturbances of the immune system mainly in T-lymphocytes with subsequent loss of tolerance and production of autoantibodies.
The hallmark of SS is the lymphocytic infiltration in the salivary and lacrimal glands with subsequent destruction of the glandular tissue.
The exact mechanism of autoimmunity in SS is unknown. However, previous studies have suggested hereditary, hormonal, and environmental factors in the onset and progression of this condition.

The infiltrate contains predominantly activated CD4 helper T cells and some B cells, including plasma cells that secrete antibody locally. Histological analysis of lacrimal and salivary glands shows large, persistent mononuclear cell infiltrates inside the glandular tissue.
Acinar epithelial atrophy and progressing fibrosis are also observed within glands of persons with SS, as well as disturbances in the normal cell apoptosis.
Autoantibodies directed against Ro and La ribonucleoproteins or cholinergic muscarinic receptors in salivary and lacrimal glands have been found in individuals with SS.
Xerophthalmia is a major manifestation of SS caused by diminished secretion of tears that ultimately leads to destruction of the corneal and bulbar conjunctival epithelium.
Levels of IFN-alpha are higher and may play a role in the pathogenesis of SS.
Patients with Sjogren's report dry eye and mouth, and may have loss of taste, bacterial and yeast infection, and increased predisposition to caries. C
If clinically suspected, order CBC, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody (ANA), and anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies. C

American College of Rheumatology criteria requires two of the following three for case definition: (1) positive anti-SSA and/or anti-SSB or positive rheumatoid factor and ANA titre >1:320, (2) ocular staining score of >3, and (3) presence of focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with a focus score >1 focus/4 mm2 in labial salivary gland biopsy. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Persistent dry cough, peripheral lymph nodes, fatigue, weight loss, and fever
Cardiac involvement is common, often GI complains such as diarrhea and malabsorption
History of radiation therapy for head and neck cancer
Fatigue, diplopia, visual loss, hemiparesis, focal weakness, and trigeminal neuralgia
Different pattern of ANA (rare occurrence of anti-SSA) and different histocompatibility antigen

list.listitem: The American-European Consensus Group criteria from the ACR and EULAR were updated in 2016, and are based on 5 point-weighted criteria ().

Xerophthalmia is a major manifestation of Sjogren's syndrome (SS) that causes a sandy feeling, itchiness, burning sensation, and inability to tolerate smoke and light. In Schirmer's test, a small strip of filter paper is placed inside the lower eyelid. It is positive if there is less than 5 mm wetting after 5 minutes. Rose Bengal or fluorescein staining of cornea and conjunctiva may demonstrate keratoconjunctivitis sicca.
Xerostomia is also common in SS resulting in sore mouth and difficulty swallowing, talking and chewing. Unstimulated whole saliva collection is typically less than 1.5 mL in 15 minutes.
In addition to subjective symptoms of dryness, decrease in mucin production predisposes the patient to loss of taste, bacterial and yeast infection, and increased predisposition to caries.

SS is usually confined to exocrine glands. However, fatigue, general malaise, low grade fever, myalgia, and arthralgia may occur.Raynaud phenomenon is found in more than 1/3 of patients with SS. Peripheral sensory or sensory-motor neuropathy occurs in approximately 10% to 20% of patients with SS.
Drycough due to dryness of the tracheobronchial mucosa and dyspnea due to interstitial lung disease may be present.
If clinically suspected, order CBC, rheumatoid factor, ANA, and anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies.

ANA must be interpreted in the clinical context, with many false positives. Anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies are found in approximately 95% and 87% of primary Sjogren's syndrome (SS) patients, respectively. Autoantibodies to the Ro and La antigens occur in about 60% to 70% of affected individuals. Anticentromere antibodies are also associated with SS.
Minor salivary gland biopsy may show focal lymphocytic sialoadenitis, but is not routinely recommended unless the diagnosis is in doubt, and the diagnostic usefulness of this procedure is unclear.

American College of Rheumatology criteria requires two of the following three for case definition: (1) positive anti-SSA and/or anti-SSB or positive rheumatoid factor and ANA titre >1:320, (2) ocular staining score of >3, (3) presence of focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with a focus score >1 focus/4 mm2 in labial salivary gland biopsy.
Ultrasound is used to diagnose abnormalities of the salivary gland, but the reported sensitivity varies considerably, while specificity is consistently high (73%-98%).

The identification of intraepithelial B-lymphocytes in salivary gland biopsies on digital image analysis serve as an additional histopathological diagnotic tool of SS based on a small case control study.
Ultrasound guided core needle biopsy is equivalent to incisional biopsy of the parotid gland in diagnosis of SS.

Labial biopsy showed more inflammation and higher focus score as opposed to parotid gland biopsy which showed more B-lymphocytes, germinal centers and lymphoepithelial lesions. Ultimately, labial gland biopsy showed high absolute agreement in histopathological features with parotid gland biopsy indicating both glands can be used for diagnosis and classification of SS.
Tests of dry eye include direct observation, corneeal staining, the fluorescein tear break-up time, and the Schirmer 1 test or Phenol red thread test.
If Sjogren's syndrome is clinically suspected in a patient with dry mouth and/or eyes, order CBC, rheumatoid factor, ANA, anti-SS A or anti-SS B, ESR, and liver function.
Confirmatory testing can include salivary gland flow rate, tear production measurement, salivary gland scintigraphy, and parotid sialography.
Lacrimal gland biopsy and/or salivary gland biopsy are also recommended depending on each case.
First line therapies include hydroxychloroquine or methotrexate for musculoskeletal symptoms; and exercise, dehydroepiandrosterone, and hydroxychloroquine for fatigue. B
For dry eye, first line treatments include lubricants, cyclosporine, and pulsed steroids.B
Cevimeline, pilocarpine and rituximab are effective treatments for xerostomia.B

Pilocarpine and cevimeline are muscarinic agonists used in the treatment of xerostomia. Pilocarpine is the traditional treatment for Sjogren's syndrome (SS) and is effective. A typical dose of pilocarpine is 5 mg orally four times daily.

Cevimeline has a greater specificity for M3 receptors than pilocarpine, and has been effective in several randomized, placebo-controlled studies. Approximately half of the patients using cevimeline reported improved symptoms compared with 10% of the patients who used placebo. A typical dose of cevimeline is 30 mg orally thrice daily.
Side effects associated with pilocarpine and to a lesser extent cevimeline may limit use. They include urinary frequency, excessive sweating, flushing, and headache.
Other systemic therapies for increasing the salivary gland function include bromhexine, anetholetrithione, and TNF-alpha blockers.

For musculoskeletal symptoms, Sjogren Society guidelines recommend hydroxychloroquine as first line treatment, methotrexate as second line, and the combination of both as third line treatment. Other treatment options in descending order include short-term steroids, long-term steroids, leflunomide, sulfasalazine, azathioprine, and cyclosporine.

For fatigue, Sjogren Society guidelines recommend: (1) exercise, (2) dehydroepiandrosterone, and (3) hydroxychloroquine. Etanercept and infliximab are not recommended for fatigue treatment, and other TNF inhibitors had insufficient evidence.
TNF inhibitors are not recommended for treatment of sicca symptoms.

While a small RCT found a benefit of rituximab for fatigue in patients with Sjogren's, two larger RCTs with 120 and 133 patients found limited benefit early and no significant benefit at 26 week.,, A systematic review of 4 studies with 276 patients concluded that there was low to moderate quality that rituximab did not reduce fatigue or improve quality of life at 24 weeks.

Another longitudinal analysis found that repeated infusions of rituximab prevent worsening salivary gland inflammation, down-regulate genes and cytokines related to immune response, and improves glandular function, when using the novel Composite of Relevant Endpoints for Sjögren Syndrome (CRESS) and Sjögren Tool for Assessing Response (STAR) which effectively stratify patient responses to therapy based on differential biomarker modulation.
An RCT with 120 adults with Sjogren syndrome found that hydroxychloroquine was no more effective than placebo. Etanercept and lamivudine are also not effective.
A small RCT (n=30) found that the RNase Fc fusion protein "RSLV-132" significantly improved measures of fatigue.

A small RCT (n=42) found that telitacicept (a small fusion protein) was safe, well tolerated and may be efficacious in reducing disease activity score among patients with primary Sjogren's syndrome. However, a larger study is needed.

In a randomized controlled trial, icalimab (a monoclonal antibody targeting CD40) has shown a promising dose-response relationship for reducing disease activity according to the EULAR Sjogren's syndrome disease activity index (ESSDAI) at 24 weeks with 150 mg and 600 mg doses showing statistical significant improvement compared to placebo.

Another RCT showed that Ianalumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting B-cell activating factor receptor (BAFF-R), demonstrated good tolerability and sustained efficacy over 52 weeks with improvements in the EULAR Sjogren's Syndrome Patient Reported Index (ESSPRI).

Dazodalibep, a novel non-antibody fusion protein, is a CD40 ligand antagonist and has also shown significant improvement in both ESSDAI and ESSPRI scores in patients with moderate to severe systemic disease activity and symptom burden. It has shown a favorable safety profile.
Oral omega-6 essential fatty acids were effective at improving ocular symptoms and tear production in a small RCT.
There is no cure for Sjögren's syndrome (SS). Treatment is usually symptomatic and supportive, including moisturizing mouthwashes, chewing gums, and salivary substitutes.
Patients should also increase fluid intake, use of moisturizers, stop smoking, use humidifiers indoors, and have regular dental checkups.

An RCT randomized patients with SS to no irrigation (control), sialendoscopy to irrigate the major salivary glands with saline, or irrigation with saline followed by triamcinoline. Both sialendoscopy groups had similar improvements in saliva flow and symptoms scores compared to the control group.

Treatment of dry eye without meibomian gland disease depends on severity. Severity level 1: education, environmental and medications changes, artificial tears and ointments. Severity level 2: cyclosporine, pulse steroids, punctal plugs, secretagogues, and moisture chamber spectacles. Severity level 3: Topical autologous serum, contact lenses, permanent punctal occlusion. Severity level 4: systemic anti-inflammatories, eyelid surgery. Evidence is generally rated good by the Sjogren Society Guidelines. With meibomian gland disease, therapies such as warm compresses, massage, and expression of meibomian glands is added.

A randomized, double-blind clinical study comparing autologous serum (AS) and platelet-rich plasma (PRP) eye drops for treating dry eye in primary Sjögren's syndrome found that both treatments significantly improved corneal and conjunctival staining scores and tear film break-up time (TBUT) at 4 and 12 weeks, with no significant differences between the groups, suggesting PRP as a good alternative due to its shorter preparation time.

A triple-blinded clinical trial investigated the effects of adipose-derived stem cell (ADSC) treatment on SS and found that ADSCs significantly improved salivary and lacrimal gland function, improving sicca symptoms and also reduced immunological and inflammatory markers. The study suggests ADSCs can effectively alleviate both systemic and subjective symptoms of pSS in a relatively short time by modulating lymphocyte proliferation, highlighting ADSC therapy as a promising approach with minimal adverse effects.
"Laughter therapy" was shown in a randomized trial with 299 patients to improve symptoms of dry eye in adults. Instructions can be found here.
Cathepsin S inhibition was not found to be beneficial in the management of SS in a randomized trial with 75 patients.
Patients with Sjögren syndrome (SS) are at increased risk of developing lymphoproliferative disorders, including lymphadenopathy and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (prevalence 2.5%-6%).B
Ocular complications include corneal ulceration, vascularization, and opacification usually worse with the progress of the condition. B
Dry mouth (85%) and caries are key factors in the overall quality of life of patients with SS. Follow up with primary dentist is highly recommended. B
Chronic pain (defined as daily pain for >3 months) is present in 65% of seropositive and 75% of seronegative patients with Sjogren's syndrome.
Patients with positive anti-citrullinated protein antibodies are more likely to develop rheumatoid arthritis.

feature.caption: Sjogren's Syndrome Diagnostic Criteria (2016 ACR/EULAR Classification).
feature.feature_body:
Item Points
Anti-SSA/Ro antibody positive 3
Focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with a focus score of ≥1 foci/4 mm2 3
Abnormal ocular staining score of 5 or more (or van Bijsterveld score of 4 or more) 1
Schirmer's test result of ≤5 mm/5 minutes 1
Unstimulated salivary flow rate ≤0.1 ml/minute 1
Total:
Primary Sjogren's syndrome is diagnosed in persons with signs and symptoms suggetive of SS who have 4 or more points.
